chunks: "The main advantage of a stepper is that it gives accurate, repeatable positioning without feedback.
Compared with a brushed or BLDC motor, which spins at a speed set by voltage and needs an encoder and a control loop to hit a position, a stepper moves a fixed angle per pulse.
So I get a position-controlled actuator with just a driver and a microcontroller, no encoder, no tuning, and low cost.
Second, holding torque: a stepper holds position at zero speed with full torque, and the error doesn't accumulate; a DC motor has to be held by a feedback loop or a brake.
Third, high torque at low speed, so I can often drive a load directly, a lead screw or a belt, without a gearbox.
Fourth, no brushes, so long life and little maintenance, and it's rugged and simple to control with step and direction signals.

The honest downsides: torque falls with speed, so they're for low to moderate speed; they draw full current when idle, so they run warm and are inefficient; they can resonate, they're noisy at some speeds, and if overloaded they miss steps silently because there's no feedback.
A servo or BLDC with an encoder wins on speed, efficiency, dynamic response and knowing where it is; a stepper wins on cost and simplicity for low-speed positioning."
